annul

uh-NUL · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To annul is to declare something legally invalid, as though it never existed.

The court agreed to annul the contract after discovering both parties had been misled.

Example

A marriage can be annulled rather than divorced if certain legal conditions were never actually met.

This wasn't simply ending an agreement -- it was declaring that, legally, it had never truly existed at all, which is exactly annul.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

invalidate: To invalidate is to make something stop counting legally, often because a flaw turns up — a missing signature, a broken rule. To annul goes further: a court's formal act that erases the thing as though it never legally existed at all. A flaw can invalidate a ballot; only a formal ruling annuls a marriage.

void: To void something is to declare it without legal force, so that it binds no one. To annul is the formal proceeding — used above all for marriages and contracts — that erases something's entire legal history, as if it had never been made. Void names the powerless status; annul names the official act of erasure.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ratify: give official approval to something, making it valid

Where it sits · how completely its existence is erased — cancel → annul → expunge

cancel vs. annul: Canceling an agreement simply ends it going forward; annulling it declares that, legally, it never existed at all.

expunge vs. annul: Expunging goes a step beyond annulling: an annulled contract is declared never to have legally existed, yet the paperwork about it stays on file, while expunging erases every record of it, as if the file itself had never been written.

root — nul

root — nul: none, nothing (Latin (nullus))

Put it together

Put it together: Annul comes from Latin ad- ('to') + nullus ('none') -- literally 'to reduce to nothing.'
